title: Is the Four-Day Week the Future?
text:
In recent years, several companies in Europe have experimented with a four-day working week, in which employees work 32 hours instead of 40 but receive the same salary. Supporters argue that this arrangement improves well-being without reducing productivity. Critics, on the other hand, claim it is unrealistic for many sectors.

The results of the largest trial so far, carried out in the UK in 2022, were surprisingly positive. Of the 61 participating companies, the vast majority decided to continue with the new schedule. Employees reported lower levels of stress and burnout, and many firms found that sick days had dropped significantly. Interestingly, revenue remained broadly the same.

Nevertheless, the model is not suitable for everyone. Hospitals, schools and factories cannot simply close one day a week; they would need to hire additional staff, which would increase costs. Moreover, some workers found that they had to squeeze the same amount of work into fewer hours, which made their days more intense. Had the trial lasted longer, researchers argue, we would have a clearer picture of the long-term effects.
